description: Usually starts with a quick “kw,” as in English “quick.” In quota, it sounds roughly like “KWAH”; in quociente, more like “kwoo.” Avoid pronouncing it like English “quote.”

thoughts: In European Portuguese, “ai” is usually a single gliding sound, not two separate vowels.
description: Pronounce “ai” like the vowel in English “eye”: start with an open “ah” sound and glide toward “ee.” Keep the glide within one syllable.

thoughts: In European Portuguese, the written sequence “au” normally forms one diphthong, much like a familiar English sound.
description: Say “ow” as in English “cow”: start with an open ah-like sound and glide toward “oo,” keeping it in one syllable.

thoughts: In European Portuguese, written “ei” is usually a diphthong. Its starting vowel varies by region, so it does not always sound like English “ay.”
description: Start with a short vowel and glide into an “ee” sound. In much of Portugal, the start sounds somewhat like “uh,” making it roughly “uh-ee”; in some regions it sounds closer to English “ay.”

thoughts: In European Portuguese, the unaccented letter sequence “eu” usually represents one gliding sound, /ew/, whether it appears at the start or end of a word.
description: Start with an “eh” sound and glide quickly toward “oo,” without making two separate syllables. It is not the English “you” sound.

thoughts: In European Portuguese, written “ou” is usually pronounced as one vowel, even though it contains two letters. Some regional accents preserve a slight glide.
description: Usually say “oh,” as in “go,” but keep the vowel steady rather than adding a strong English-style glide. In some regional accents, it sounds closer to “oh-oo.”

thoughts: The letters “ui” do not always represent one sound in European Portuguese: the preceding consonant and the word’s spelling affect the pronunciation.
description: In “Rui,” it sounds roughly like English “roo-ee,” said quickly. In “guitarra,” the u is silent, so “gui” sounds like “gee.” In “pinguim,” the u sounds like English w, giving “gwim,” with a nasal vowel.

thoughts: The spelling “am” changes sound according to its position: compare drama, samba, and the verb ending in programam.
description: Before a vowel, “am” can sound like an ordinary a followed by m, as in drama. Before a consonant, the a is usually nasal: let air pass through your nose rather than clearly saying an m, as in samba. At the end of a verb, unstressed “-am” sounds roughly like a nasal “ow,” as in programam.

thoughts: The spelling “an” does not always represent the same sound: the following letter determines whether the vowel is nasal.
description: Before a consonant, “an” usually represents a nasal vowel: say an ‘ah’-like sound through both your mouth and nose, without a separate English-style ‘n’. Before another vowel, pronounce the ‘a’ and ‘n’ separately, as in “banana.”

thoughts: In European Portuguese, “em” has two common pronunciations: a nasal vowel before a consonant and a nasal diphthong at the end of a word.
description: Before a consonant, as in “tempo,” it sounds roughly like the vowel in “ten,” but nasalized: let some air escape through your nose without pronouncing a separate m. At the end of a word, as in “item,” it sounds more like a nasal “eye” with a softened ending.

thoughts: In European Portuguese, written “en” usually signals a nasal vowel before a consonant. When the n begins the next syllable, the e and n are pronounced separately.
description: Before a consonant, “en” sounds roughly like the vowel in English “bed” said through the nose, without a distinct final n. Before a vowel, the n starts the next syllable; the e may be a very short, reduced vowel, as in “menu.”

thoughts: The spelling “im” has two main readings: a nasal vowel when the m closes a syllable, and an ordinary i followed by an m sound when the m begins the next syllable.
description: Before a consonant or at the end of a word, “im” sounds roughly like English “eem” with the vowel pronounced through the nose and little or no final m. Before a vowel, pronounce the i and m separately, as in “image.”

thoughts: The spelling “in” can represent either a nasal vowel or an oral vowel followed by an n sound, depending on what follows.
description: Before a consonant, “in” is usually a nasal ‘ee’ sound: let some air pass through your nose rather than pronouncing a separate n. Before a vowel, pronounce the i and n separately, as in “cinema.” In “inh,” the n belongs to “nh,” which sounds roughly like ‘ny.’

thoughts: In European Portuguese, “om” usually marks a nasal vowel, whether it appears before a consonant or at the end of a word.
description: Say an “oh”-like vowel while letting some air pass through your nose. Do not pronounce the m as a separate sound, as you would in English “home.”

thoughts: The spelling “on” does not always represent the same sound. Before a consonant, the n usually makes the o nasal; before a vowel, the n begins the next syllable.
description: Before a consonant, pronounce “on” as a nasal vowel: let air pass through your nose, without finishing with an English-style n. Before a vowel, pronounce the n separately; in an unstressed syllable, the o may sound like “oo.”

thoughts: The spelling “um” can represent a nasal vowel or an ordinary vowel followed by an m, depending on where it occurs.
description: At the end of a word, “um” usually sounds like a nasal ‘oo’: say ‘oo’ while letting air flow through your nose, without a distinct final m. Before another vowel, as in “perfume,” the u sounds like ‘oo’ and the m begins the next syllable.

thoughts: The spelling “un” has two main pronunciations: a nasal vowel before a consonant, or a separate “u” and “n” before a vowel.
description: Before a consonant, “un” usually sounds like a nasal “oo”: say “oo” while letting air flow through your nose, without a distinct “n” sound. Before a vowel, as in “universo,” pronounce “u” and “n” separately, roughly “oo-n.”

description: At the end of a word, s usually sounds like English “sh” before a pause or a voiceless consonant. Before a voiced consonant, it sounds like the “s” in “measure.” Before a vowel, it links to the next word and sounds like “z.”
